endorsements.quote: The most important governance principle is having a well-rounded team at all levels and not just diversity in the dataset.
Additionally, accountability for algorithmic outcomes must be assigned to specific individuals and/or governance bodies so as to not allow failures to go unaddressed or ignored.

In the data collection phase, there must be a conscious effort to gather that reflects real-world complexity, including factors like gender, race, ethnicity, age, socioeconomic status, rather than relying on a limited search through institutional archives that typically yield a skewed dataset.

Whereas workforce training programs should include a discussion of the risks of AI such as algorithmic biases, it should also highlight general guidelines on how to identify, report, and mitigate against these biases.
Finally, if multiple algorithms are being deployed, introduce the algorithms gradually and carefully instead of simultaneously in order to monitor the output in each instance.

When purchasing an AI platform, it is fundamental to validate it against the specific population in which it will operate and work with diverse communities to ensure that the algorithm is helpful and not harmful.

Human supervision reduces the risk of feeding the model biased data, thereby minimizing hidden outcomes, and more importantly, the human must have a very clear and easy way to terminate model operation when the outcome is malicious.

Finally, there must be mechanisms (standard operating procedure or service ticketing system) for end-users (e.g., pathologists) and subjects (e.g., patients) to provide feedback regarding model outcomes.
Model outputs should be validated using stratified K-fold cross-validation or bootstrapping specifically applied for underrepresented variables.
After deployment, the quality control matrix should be tracked to make sure that the model behaves the way it is intended in each population.
Once this auditability is established, there must be a clear mechanism for accountability, whereby governance entities can be held accountable when the model produces malicious output.
AI models cannot be integrated in clinical workflows without monitoring and quality control measures.

unlisted_practices: Appoint a representation champion embedded in the AI development team to coordinate balanced representation across the data lifecycle.
Prefer augmented (human-in-the-loop) AI over autonomous AI.
Pathology departments should encourage development of AI tools that advance equity.
Harmonize laboratory data across assay platforms and account for preanalytical variables when aggregating data for model training.
Run reference cases through the deployed algorithm each shift and escalate deviations below accuracy thresholds to leadership for recalibration.
End parachute science by returning benefit and building research capacity in communities whose data are used.
Remove bias-introducing information from residency application review using standardized merit-based rubrics.
Consider synthetic data generation only as a last resort when real-world representation cannot be achieved.

screen.reason: The paper proposes an ethical framework and guidelines for addressing demographic bias and representation in deploying AI in pathology.
